newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: U.S. citizen accused of spying grilled in S.Korea.
newsitem.headline: U.S. citizen accused of spying grilled in S.Korea.

text.p: South Korean intelligence and military officials on Thursday began questioning a U.S. businessman arrested for spying, a Seoul official said.
Donald Ratcliffe, 62, was arrested on Wednesday by the Agency for National Security Planning on suspicion of collecting military secrets.

An agency spokesman said the executive for U.S.-based Litton Guidance and Controls Systems was being questioned, but declined to say where he was being held. Ratcliffe's company is a division of defence contractor Litton Industries Inc.
The Chosun Ilbo newspaper said the country's top intelligence agency planned to question Ratcliffe on whether he passed military secrets to the U.S. government.

Yonhap Television News linked Ratcliffe's case to the arrest last September of Robert Kim, a Korean-born U.S. citizen charged with passing more than 40 classified documents to a South Korean embassy official.

Kim, 56, was a U.S. Navy computer specialist who became a U.S. citizen in 1974. His arrest sparked indignation among many South Koreans, who viewed it as a snub of an old ally even though Kim was not a South Korean citizen.
South Korea's foreign ministry spokesman denied any connection between the cases.
"I am certain that his (Ratcliffe's) case will be handled fairly and according to the law," said Lee Kyu-hyung. He added that the U.S. so far had made no request to interview Ratcliffe.
In Washington, U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters on Wednesday he was aware of reports an American had been held but said he was unable to give any details.

"You can be assured that our embassy in Seoul is following this case. We have an obligation to this individual, to try to advise him of his rights and to provide all necessary consular assistance to him."
A U.S. embassy spokesman in Seoul declined to comment.
Ratcliffe, the director of Asian operations for his company, was arrested outside the main U.S. military base in Seoul, the Chosun Ilbo reported.
U.S. military spokesman Jim Coles said Ratcliffe had a pass to the Yongsan base as he was a military retiree. He was staying at a hotel on the facility.
The Dong-A Ilbo daily said Ratcliffe was suspected of having collected information on Seoul's arms procurements programme, but it gave no source for the report.
South Korea plans billions of dollars of military purchases, including fighter jets and air defence systems, over the next several years.
The United States, which Seoul has looked to as its main supplier of military hardware, is now competing with European and Russian suppliers for lucrative contracts.
Some 37,000 U.S. troops are stationed in South Korea to protect against threats from the communist North.
